newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah slips back, ringgit choppy.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah slips back, ringgit choppy.

text.p: A semblance of calm returned to regional currency spot and forward markets on Friday afternoon after the Indonesian and Malaysian central banks denied rumours they were planning to curb swap transactions.

In Malaysia, the ringgit continued on a roller-coaster ride, spiking back up above the 2.4900 level to the dollar on news of a sharply higher than expected March trade surplus. It was quoted at 2.4850/60 to the dollar at 0225 GMT.
Malaysia posted a trade surplus of 1.75 billion ringgit in March against a revised surplus of 368.5 million in February.

The ringgit jumped sharply to a high of 2.4735 in early trade from an opening around 2.4900 as offshore players unloaded long dollar positions on talk that Bank Negara had cut off their access to the local swap market.

Rumours the Malaysian authorities were planning to stop all swap transactions added to the panic, but the market calmed somewhat after Bank Negara denied it had issued instructions to banks to stop undertaking swap transactions.
The central bank said in a statement the shortage of ringgit in the market was a temporary phonomenon resulting from speculative activities.

Dealers said it was not clear whether the central bank had indeed asked Kuala Lumpur banks to stop quoting tom/next rates to offshore parties, as the Thai central bank did on Thursday to squeeze out speculators.

But they said local banks had definitely been reluctant to quote to offshore players, pushing tom/next rates up sharply and causing funds to sell dollars on the spot market to cover their short ringgit positions.

"If you're a local bank and you see swaps are so tight, and if you're very long, you just sit back and relax and people will take you regardless of the spread," said a European bank dealer in Singapore.
He said foreign funds were still trying to get out of their positions and the dollar would be sold on any rallies against the ringgit.
In Indonesia, the rupiah settled down after a Bank Indonesia official said the central bank had no plans to ask local banks to stop quoting tom/next to offshore players.
"We have no intention to freeze the swap facility for now," Bambang Trianto, director of the central bank's foreign exchange department told Reuters.
"But we are watching the market very closely. We are comfortable with market rates," he added.
The rupiah leaped to a high of 2,413.0 from an opening of 2,444.0/45.0. It was quoted at 2,429.0/36.0 at 0625 GMT.
Panicky offshore players had swamped the swap market, driving tom/next to a high of 7.0 points, equivalent to about 100 percent interest, before they fell to 0.6/0.7 at midday.
"I think the rupiah is affected more by a spill-over from speculation in the ringgit," one dealer in Singapore said.

"Many who went long on dollars Thursday got burnt today. It's really a wild swing. I had one screen quoting swaps at 30 while the other screen was at 60. There were a lot of arbitrage opportunities," the dealer said.
Dealers said traders also focused on one-month swaps, possibly because of the campaign for the May 29 general elections, which has been marred by sporadic violence.
In Thailand, the central bank said it had been successful in fighting off speculators and baht trading had returned to normal.
Dealers in Singapore said baht forward rates had come off although talk persisted that the central bank was still not allowing foreign parties access to the local swap market.

Bank of Thailand (BOT) deputy governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said foreign speculators who sold the baht heavily for U.S. dollars would have to pay a high price by buying back the baht from the more expensive swap market to close outstanding positions.

"The speculators must pay the price. Because of their speculative move, the swap premiums soared. If they intend to buy from the forward market like that, they must buy through the swap market," he said.
Bangkok dealers confirmed the central bank had told them not to buy dollars from offshore punters to fight against further speculation.

"They're squeezing the speculators by not allowing them to obtain baht, which they've been short of. The swap rates are very expensive so it's cheaper to get funds from the cash market," a European bank dealer in Singapore said.
The Singapore dollar alone remained rock solid as players focused entirely on volatility in other Southeast Asian currencies, ignoring a slew of economic data in the city-state.
But dealers said some spillover impact was seen in the money market where liquidity tightened and pushed rates up.
"Everybody is just very scared now. They just want to cover all their positions," a U.S. bank dealer said.
-- Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221-384-6364), Anchalee Koetsawang in Bangkok (662) 652-0642 and Sonali Desai in Singapore.
